description: Be an Earth System Trend Detective! We’re a Ho Chi Minh City team building a tool that turns NASA satellite and model data (MODIS, GPM, MERRA-2) into trends anyone can explore and test for significance. We’re students passionate about climate and data. Join us to turn real Earth data into an immersive experience! We’re looking for teammates skilled in web/app development, data analysis or statistics, web or UI design, and storytelling, or simply curious about our planet.
summary:
TerraTrace is a free web app that turns a question about the Earth, such as "Is my region getting warmer?", into an honest answer in plain language. It works like a detective case. A few simple questions narrow ten NASA measurements down to the right one. The user picks a place on a 3D globe, guesses the answer, and then sees the real NASA record as a chart. The app then gives a verdict: rising, falling, mixed evidence, or no significant trend.

TerraTrace covers every step the challenge asks for: choosing a variable, getting its data for a region, drawing the time series, and reporting a rate of change with a significance test. This matters because NASA's data is open to everyone, but most people cannot tell a real change from seasons and noise. TerraTrace lets students check claims about a changing planet for themselves.
details:
TerraTrace guides a student through five screens:

  1. Clues. The app asks one question at a time, such as "What would you notice changing?". Each answer removes "suspects" until one measurement is left. There are ten: air temperature, daily high temperature, daily low temperature, surface temperature, precipitation, snowfall, relative humidity, wind speed, sunlight at the ground and cloud cover.
  2. Scene. The user picks one of 12 prepared regions on a 3D globe, or types the coordinates of any point on Earth. For 10 of the regions the app has a lead: a hint of what to check there, with a link to the NASA article behind it. The lead appears when it is about the measurement the user chose.
  3. Case brief. The app reads the question back, for example "You want to know whether air temperature in the Tibetan Plateau has changed since 1981. Is that right?". The user then guesses: rising, falling or no change.
  4. Evidence. A chart shows the monthly record with a trend line. One switch removes the seasonal cycle, and a picker limits the analysis to any span of at least 10 years.
  5. Verdict. One plain sentence gives the result and its rate, says whether the guess was right, and adds a caution. The user can then compare a second region side by side.

Two solved cases open in one click. In one of them, the app finds that air temperature on the Tibetan Plateau has risen by about 0.23 °C per decade since 1981 (p-value below 0.001; 95% interval +0.17 to +0.28 °C).

How it works

All the data is monthly values from NASA POWER. A prepared region uses the average of 9 points sampled inside the region, weighted by the area each point stands for. A typed point is fetched live from POWER. The statistics run in the user's browser, so there is no server of ours and no account:

  • The Mann-Kendall test says whether there is a steady upward or downward drift. With the seasonal cycle removed, the app uses the seasonal Mann-Kendall test, which compares each month only with the same month in other years.
  • Sen's slope gives the rate of change per decade. One odd year barely moves it.
  • A straight-line fit gives a 95% interval for that rate.

The app calls a change "rising" or "falling" only when the test is significant (p-value below 0.05) and the interval excludes zero on the same side as the rate. If only one of the two holds, the verdict is "mixed evidence". "No significant trend" is shown as a real result, not a failure. A record with fewer than 120 months of values gets no verdict, and the app says why.

We checked our statistics against two standard tools, pyMannKendall and SciPy. The p-values agree to 3 decimal places, and the rates and intervals agree to 6. The project has 329 automated tests.

Benefits

  • It gives a verdict in everyday words, not only a chart.
  • It is honest about its limits. Every verdict warns that neighbouring months are related, which can make a trend look more certain than it is. The app reports whether something changed, never why, and it does not predict the future.
  • Guessing first and then seeing the evidence teaches students to doubt a line that merely goes up.
  • It needs no login, no install and no expertise. It works on phones, tablets and computers, and we checked it for keyboard use, colour contrast and 200% zoom.
  • No AI model runs in the app, so the same question always gives the same answer.

What we hope to achieve

We want students, teachers and curious people to test claims about a changing planet with real NASA data, and to learn what a trustworthy trend looks like. Our next steps would be true area averages from more NASA products, trends that are not straight lines, and regions that the user draws.

Tools, languages and software

  • The app: TypeScript, React, Vite, Observable Plot for the charts and three.js for the globe, tested with Vitest and Testing Library.
  • Data preparation and test series: Python with NumPy, SciPy, pyMannKendall, requests and pytest.
  • Hosting: a static site on GitHub Pages, built and tested by GitHub Actions.
  • The code is open source under the Apache-2.0 licence: https://github.com/Andrew1013-development/TerraTrace

Parts of the code, tests and documents were written with AI assistance (Claude and Claude Code, by Anthropic). A developer reviewed every AI-drafted change, and each use is listed in AI_USE.md in the repository.
